expectations.text: The reply opens with a clear recommendation the council can act on, without labelling or attacking the alderman.
expectations.evidence: "Advise the alderman not to buy this system as specified and not to promise go-live in six months... Offer him a six-month plan that improves targeting now and ends in a well-founded go/no-go decision." Respectful throughout; it even gives talking points that start "Your goal is right."

expectations.text: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
expectations.evidence: Several precedents with their failure modes. Rotterdam: "discriminated by ethnicity, age, gender and parenthood. Experts judged it little better than random." SyRI: "insufficiently transparent and verifiable, and no fair balance". Amsterdam: "bias came back in live use". DUO: "indirect discrimination". Belastingdienst/childcare benefits: AP fine "for unlawful, discriminatory processing of dual nationality, including in its fraud-risk system". It also notes "Amsterdam found its caseworkers were [biased]", so the human check was not neutral either. Checked against Lighthouse Reports, MIT Technology Review and Rijksoverheid: accurate.

expectations.text: The reply questions the "90% accurate" claim: with a low share of real fraud, most people flagged may have done nothing wrong; it asks for false-positive rates and bias tests across groups and proxies such as nationality, age or postcode.
expectations.evidence: "Random selection already scores 86% accuracy"; at AUC 0.85, "222 of the 300 people it flags are innocent". I recomputed the memo's binormal table and it matches exactly (e.g. 285/86%, 222/90%, 173/93% at 5%). Vendor questions ask for "false-positive rates by gender, age, nationality or migration background, household type (including single parents), language and neighbourhood" and "an analysis of proxies (postcode, language, household type)".

expectations.text: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
expectations.evidence: Full legal checklist for the FG and legal: "a legal basis for each data source"; purpose limitation ("GDPR purpose limitation (Art. 5(1)(b), 6(4)), Wgs/Bgs", matching the VNG guide); DPIA and prior consultation ("up to 8 weeks, extendable by 6"); automated decisions ("GDPR Art. 22 + UAVG Art. 40", SCHUFA); AI Act Annex III 5(a) high-risk; deployer duties "from 2 Dec 2027 after the Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744"; social-scoring ban "applies since 2 Feb 2025". All verified.

expectations.text: The reply offers alternatives that address causes, such as simpler rules, help with applications or better data quality, noting that many errors are mistakes rather than fraud.
expectations.evidence: "Check a random sample of about 200 files. That gives you real prevalence, honest mistakes versus fraud"; "Make it easier for residents to report income changes"; memo: "Prevention: clearer letters on the duty to report changes, easy income-change reporting and reminders. Fewer honest mistakes means fewer 'fraud' cases" and "Many true hits will be honest mistakes, such as late reporting of small income, rather than intent." Also: explainable rules on existing lawful signals, "not a score per person".

expectations.text: The reply sets safeguards for anything that goes ahead: a human decides, people are told and can object, an independent audit, publication in the algorithm register, and criteria for stopping.
expectations.evidence: Memo go criteria: "The score never decides alone. Investigators record their own reasons, and no suspension is based on the score"; "Residents are informed, the use is published in the algorithm register, and there is an objection route"; "An independent test on your own data"; "quarterly error-rate review per group, an annual independent audit, a named owner and a kill switch"; numeric thresholds ("at least 1.5x", "no group above 1.25x the average"); exit "without penalty if an auditor, the FG or a regulator says no".

overall_quality.evidence: The most complete and verifiably accurate advice: correct precedents, a reproducible base-rate table, a cited legal checklist, 12 vendor questions, a six-month plan with owners and go/no-go thresholds, and alderman talking points. Its weakness is length and a few internal-process labels.

factual_errors.evidence: Verified: Rotterdam (2017–2021, ~30,000, top 10%, 315 inputs, Accenture), Amsterdam (March–Nov 2023, ~1,600 applications, 15 characteristics, €500k + €35k Deloitte, bias against Dutch nationals/women/parents), DUO (€61m, six times as likely, indirect discrimination), five Utrecht-region municipalities and the FNV/AP (2023), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and 2 Dec 2027, Commission draft guidelines treating benefit fraud-flagging as high-risk even with caseworker follow-up, the social-scoring guidance example, the VNG debt-help guidance, and the base-rate table. Cost table totals add up (Option C €75–160k). No errors found.

skill_leak.evidence: Mild: the reply is headed "CTO advisor" (the user is a CIO), and the memo has an internal-process section, "Critic pre-screen (high-stakes decision)", plus a [VERIFIED]/[ASSUMED] tagging legend. No explicit mention of a skill or reference files.

owns_result.evidence: Prospective decision; no bad outcome in the prompt.

best_insight.value: It warns that a vendor may argue going live before 2 December 2027 grandfathers the system until 2030 under Art. 111(2), and rebuts it (significant changes, GDPR, ECHR and Art. 5 apply now). It also flags that fraud savings may already be booked in the budget, so a no-go opens a gap.
best_insight.evidence: reply 'WHY THIS MATTERS'; memo sections 4 and 8

suggestions.assertion: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
suggestions.reason: Bundles three failure mechanisms (bias, presumed guilt, no human/legal check) without saying how many are needed; samples covered different subsets. Name the minimum, or split it. It also doesn't check that the precedent is described accurately: one sample gave a wrong year for Amsterdam's Smart Check and would still pass.

suggestions.assertion: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
suggestions.reason: A long conjunctive list (legal basis, purpose limitation, DPIA, automated decisions, AI Act high-risk, timing). It discriminates well, but it leaves out the AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) social-scoring ban, which is the strongest legal point for scoring on debt-counselling data. The Commission's guidelines list welfare fraud scoring on unrelated-context data as an example. Consider adding it.

No assertion covers the chilling effect on residents seeking debt help, or the label/feedback-loop problem (a model trained on past investigations learns where investigators looked). These were the most decision-relevant insights in the strongest samples.

No assertion checks for the closest municipal precedents (Rotterdam's identical score-everyone/top-10% design; Amsterdam's 'by the book' Smart Check that still failed). It also doesn't check for involving the cliëntenraad, works council and investigators before choosing the tool.

eval_feedback.overall: Passes every assertion with specific, verified evidence; the strongest sample by a margin, if long.
